algorithm.Title: Diabetes - High Blood Sugar - Male (Adult)
algorithm.ContentSet: IST Open-Source Guideline Content | Adult | Male
Definition: Hyperglycemia (high blood sugar) and diabetic ketoacidosis risk assessment decomposed from NHS.UK's published when-to-get-help guidance.

KeyPoints: Hyperglycaemia mainly affects people with diabetes and can become serious if untreated.
Common symptoms include thirst, frequent urination, weakness or tiredness, blurred vision, and weight loss.
Vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, drowsiness, fruity breath, confusion, or high ketones can indicate a life-threatening complication.
Background.ExpertReviewer: PENDING: Qatar adult, pediatric, obstetric, diabetes, emergency, and nursing governance review

FirstAid: Call Qatar emergency services on 999 and do not drive for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep/rapid breathing, fruity breath, dehydration, confusion/drowsiness, ketones above the person's emergency-plan threshold, or rapid deterioration. Follow only the person's prescribed sick-day/pump plan; do not improvise extra insulin. Do not force fluids when vomiting, drowsy, or unsafe to swallow, and do not delay 999 for another glucose or ketone check. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care.

questions.Question: Is the measured glucose below 4 mmol/L, or are shaking, sweating, hunger, or confusion suggesting hypoglycaemia?
questions.Information: A low reading or hypo symptom pattern belongs in the low-blood-sugar pathway and needs prompt treatment.

questions.Question: Along with high blood sugar, is there nausea/vomiting or stomach pain, faster-than-usual breathing or heart rate, drowsiness, breath with a fruity ('pear drop') smell, confusion or difficulty concentrating, or a high ketone level?
questions.Information: NHS.UK high blood sugar guidance lists these as emergency ambulance or Emergency Department criteria for possible diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Do not self-drive to the Emergency Department - call an ambulance.

questions.Question: Has blood sugar remained high or symptoms continued despite trying to lower it, or is this high blood sugar in someone not previously diagnosed with diabetes?
questions.Information: NHS.UK guidance recommends contacting a diabetes care team or primary-care clinician for persistent high readings or a new, undiagnosed presentation.

advice.Title: Qatar emergency hyperglycaemia/DKA response
Content: Call Qatar emergency services on 999 and do not drive for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep/rapid breathing, fruity breath, dehydration, confusion/drowsiness, ketones above the person's emergency-plan threshold, or rapid deterioration. Follow only the person's prescribed sick-day/pump plan; do not improvise extra insulin. Do not force fluids when vomiting, drowsy, or unsafe to swallow, and do not delay 999 for another glucose or ketone check. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care.
Call Back If: worsening drowsiness or confusion; vomiting, abnormal breathing, or dehydration; rising ketones or failure of the personal plan.

advice.Title: Routine high blood sugar follow-up
Content: Take diabetes medicine as prescribed, avoid sugary/starchy foods, manage stress, stay active, and follow sick-day guidance from the diabetes care team.
Call Back If: nausea, vomiting, or confusion develops; breath develops a fruity smell.

references: NHS.UK, "High blood sugar (hyperglycaemia)", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/high-blood-sugar-hyperglycaemia/ (page last reviewed 17 March 2026)
